analysis.one_liner: Caps pay for temporary foreign farmworkers and eases rules for the farm employers who hire them.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let farm employers pay H-2A guest workers as little as 115% of the minimum wage — far below the current required farm wage rate — never got a hearing or a vote and died in the House Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The BARN Act would rewrite the H-2A program that brings temporary foreign agricultural workers to U.S. farms. It would cap employer pay for these workers at 115% of the federal or state minimum wage (currently about $8.34 an hour federally, versus the ~$17-19 an hour the program requires today), delete a rule requiring employers to hire qualified U.S. applicants before turning the job over to a guest worker, move the program from the Labor Department to the Agriculture Department, and auto-approve any visa application the new agency fails to decide within 15 days. It would also let employers in some states pay a housing allowance instead of providing free housing, and would restrict federally funded legal aid to farmworkers.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural employers who hire H-2A guest workers. They would gain a hard ceiling on wages (roughly half of today's required rate in many states), no obligation to consider U.S. applicants for half the job period, faster approvals with automatic approval if the Agriculture Department misses a 15-day deadline, and the option to swap free employer-provided housing for a cash allowance. Employers would also be shielded from legal-aid groups entering their property uninvited.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the wage an H-2A employer must pay at 115% of the federal or applicable state minimum wage — about $8.34 an hour federally, versus the program's current Adverse Effect Wage Rate of roughly $17 or more in most states.
Eliminates the 50% rule, which currently requires an H-2A employer to keep hiring any qualified U.S. applicants until half the guest worker's contract period has elapsed.

Moves the program from the Department of Labor, whose mission includes protecting workers, to the Department of Agriculture, and requires a decision within 15 days of filing — with the application deemed approved automatically if the deadline is missed.

Lets employers in states where a governor certifies adequate housing pay a cash housing allowance instead of providing free housing, and says an employer providing an allowance is not a 'housing provider' under the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act.

Bars the Legal Services Corporation from helping farmworkers unless they are present in the U.S. and the parties have tried mediation, and says employers do not have to let legal-aid staff onto their property without a pre-arranged appointment with a specific worker.

analysis.who_pays: H-2A guest workers, whose pay could be cut to near the minimum wage and whose access to free housing and legal help would shrink, and U.S. farmworkers, who would lose the 50% rule that keeps employers looking for domestic hires before settling on guest workers. Communities with heavy farm-labor employment would face downward pressure on agricultural wages generally, since employers could replace or hold down local pay with a legal, cheaper guest-worker channel.

drawbacks.text: The wage cap would cut H-2A workers' required pay by roughly half in many states, since 115% of the $7.25 federal minimum wage is far below the Adverse Effect Wage Rate the program otherwise guarantees.
Deleting the 50% rule removes employers' obligation to hire qualified U.S. applicants during the first half of a contract, weakening the program's protection of domestic farm jobs.
Automatic approval of applications the Agriculture Department fails to decide in 15 days would strip away review of job offers, wages, and housing before workers are admitted.
Restrictions on Legal Services Corporation funding and on legal-aid visits to farms would make it harder for isolated, low-income workers to enforce whatever rights remain.
A 15-day application deadline with auto-approval, combined with a faster 30-day filing window, could strain the new administering agency and invite errors or rubber-stamping.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to agricultural employers through lower mandated wages, faster and more automatic approvals, and fewer avenues for worker enforcement. The costs fall on some of the lowest-paid workers in the country — foreign guest workers and the U.S. farmworkers competing with them — through a pay cap of roughly half today's required rate, loss of the domestic-hiring rule, and reduced access to housing and legal help. There is no provision in the bill that compensates workers for these losses.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Allen introduced the BARN Act on March 24, 2023.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farmworkers came out ahead: because the bill died, H-2A guest workers kept the current wage floor (the Adverse Effect Wage Rate) and U.S. farmworkers kept the 50% rule, the free-housing requirement, and access to federally funded legal aid. Agricultural employers who wanted a cheaper labor channel gained nothing.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it stayed dormant from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so there is no record of where members or parties stood.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (growers of labor-intensive crops, farm labor contractors)
industries.note: The bill would hand these employers a wage ceiling of 115% of the minimum wage — roughly half the current required farm wage rate — plus automatic visa approvals, an end to the 50% rule requiring them to consider U.S. applicants, and an option to swap free housing for a cash allowance. Its gain comes directly out of farmworkers' pay and protections.

industries.industry: H-2A guest workers and domestic farm laborers
industries.note: These are the workers whose pay, housing, and access to legal help the bill would cut; they are ordinary working people, not an industry, but they bear the bill's direct costs.

industries.industry: Legal aid organizations (Legal Services Corporation grantees)
industries.note: The bill would restrict LSC-funded legal help for farmworkers and bar legal-aid staff from employer property without a pre-arranged appointment, limiting these groups' ability to represent isolated low-wage workers.
